title: Presentation and portal design direction
summary: Three design decisions shown as rendered candidates in every skin and mode: page anatomy, one type scale, figure colour; choose one per part.

blocks.markdown:
**What this is.** The design direction for cf-present documents and docs-portal pages, in three parts: how a page opens, one type scale, and how figures use colour. Each part shows rendered candidates; switch skin and appearance in Settings to see them in all six pairs.

**Why now.** Figures render nearly grey because the grammar reserves accent for six marks; comparison and decision titles render larger than the subsection around them; the document summary never reaches the page.

**Where it stands.** Candidates only. No token, style or test has changed; the tokens stay byte-identical until you choose.

**What you decide.** One candidate per part below, or a direction of your own in the notes. The recommended option is marked on each question.

## Part 1: how a page opens

The page head and every section lead with context. Today the title lives only in the top bar and the summary never shows. Both candidates put the title, the summary and a meta line at the top of the document column and give every section heading a lead; they differ in how a section announces itself.

## Part 2: one type scale

The document title must be larger than a section, a section larger than a subsection, and a subsection larger than any block title. Today a comparison column title and the decision title render at 18.4 px against a 17.9 px subsection. Both candidates fix the order; they differ in how far apart the steps sit.

blocks.title: Three scales, measured in px at the default size
blocks.caption: S1 is the kit scale the portal already uses; S2 widens every step to about 1.33 so the order survives the compact size and reads at a glance.

## Part 3: how figures use colour

The governing path of every figure is drawn in accent; everything else is grey for context. Today only six marks carry accent, so a structure figure, a layering figure with no act marker and every coverage figure render grey. The four figures below are the same in every candidate; only their colour rules change. The first four are drawn by the runtime from their declarations as the grammar draws them today.

figure.question: Where does a skill live, and what keeps the copies honest?
figure.idea: One source, four managed copies, and a test that compares bytes.
figure.title: Where a skill lives and what keeps its copies identical
figure.description: Three regions. The owner region assets/base holds the skill source. The live region holds two copies, .claude/skills and .agents/skills. The baseline region .codeflow/.baseline holds the same two copies again. Solid arrows run from the source to each live copy and from each live copy to its baseline copy, meaning managed copy. A dashed line with open square ends runs under all regions, meaning the parity test compares every copy with the source byte for byte.
figure.caption: Edit the source under assets/base only; the four copies are written by the scaffold and a test fails the build when any copy drifts.

draw.text: parity test: bytes equal, or the build fails
parity test: bytes equal, or the build fails

figure.question: Which plane covers which moment, and which one is the boundary?
figure.idea: Four planes cover a change in order, and only the remote one is a boundary.
figure.title: Four enforcement planes along the life of one change
figure.description: A shared axis runs edit, commit, push, pull request, merge. Git hooks cover commit and push and can stop the change at both. The session git-guard covers every moment from edit to merge and can stop the change at commit, push, pull request and merge, because it also reads gh pr create and gh pr merge. CI covers push and pull request and can stop the change at the pull request, where its checks run and run again on every push to the open pull request. Remote branch protection covers push, pull request and merge, can stop the change at push and at merge, and is the only plane drawn with an end cap, meaning remote and required here. At push three planes can act; CI acts once the pull request is open.
figure.caption: Hooks and the guard stop changes before push; CI blocks the pull request; verified remote protection stops push and merge.

figure.question: What does an agent ask, and of whom, before its first edit?
figure.idea: Three calls and two answers come before the first edit, and one answer can refuse.
figure.title: The exchanges that come before the first edit
figure.description: Three lifelines: agent, git, codeflow. Time runs down. The agent calls git worktree list and git answers with the paths and branches. The agent decides identity and intent match, a human decision ring. The agent calls git fetch origin and decides currency. The agent calls codeflow work start TSK-NNN; codeflow answers anchored, or refuses at a stop bar. The first edit follows the answer.
figure.caption: The agent asks git where it is and whether it is current, then asks codeflow whether the task is anchored, and edits nothing until the last answer is yes.

facts.claim: identity, intent-match and currency precede the first mutation
codeflow work start proves the task is anchored before product edits

draw.text: currency: base is the target tip
currency: base is the target tip

figure.question: Which plane enforces which rule, and is any rule unclaimed?
figure.idea: Every rule has at least one plane; the ticket rule is not claimed remotely.
figure.title: Which plane enforces which rule
figure.description: A grid of five rules against four planes. Secret scan: hooks covered, guard covered, CI covered, remote covered. Protected branch push: hooks covered, guard covered, CI not applicable, remote covered. No AI attribution: hooks covered, guard covered, CI covered, remote not applicable. Breaking change footer: hooks partial, guard not run, CI covered, remote not applicable. Ticket reference: hooks covered, guard not applicable, CI partial, remote not claimed.
figure.caption: Every rule is enforced by at least one plane, and the one crossed cell is a claim no plane makes.

facts.derive: the rules named in Git rules and the four planes

check.text: Four planes provide defense in depth

blocks.title: C1: accent governs
blocks.caption: Tokens stay byte-identical; one governing region per figure takes the accent-soft field with an accent edge, and the covered cell takes the accent.

blocks.title: C2: accent and two companions
blocks.caption: Two category hues per skin and mode, each with a tint, for peers that must be told apart; the governing region stays accent and every category mark keeps its dash, width or cap.

blocks.title: C3: tonal ramp
blocks.caption: Tokens stay byte-identical; two derived tints of the accent grade the regions below the governing one, so hierarchy reads in one hue.

blocks.title: C2 values proposed for tokens.json and their contrast
blocks.caption: Each ink clears 4.5 to 1 on the figure ground and the canvas; the figure ink clears 4.5 to 1 on every tint; the floors the design system sets for accent and text.

blocks.title: Which figure colour
blocks.markdown: C1 and C3 add no hue and keep tokens.json byte-identical; they add a governing-region mark and, for C3, two tints derived in figure.css. C2 adds four roles per skin and mode (two inks, two tints) to tokens.json, tokens.css, figure.css and the portal token sheet, with the drift test extended; category hue is used only for peers the subject names, never for the governing path, and never alone.

options.label: C1: accent governs, no new hue
C3: tonal ramp, no new hue

blocks.markdown:
## Part 4: a dedicated section block

The task asks whether a `section` block (title, lead) is worth adding beyond the `## ` heading pattern. Evidence from the candidates: A1 gets heading, lead and a route entry from the Markdown a narrative block already carries, styled by one rule (the paragraph after a heading is its lead). A2's plate needs a block so the number and the lead are data, which costs a schema change, validation, docs and a migration for every existing document.

blocks.title: Add a section block
blocks.markdown: The recommendation follows the anatomy choice: no block with A1, a block with A2.

options.label: No: headings in narrative blocks, lead styled by rule
Yes: a section block with title and lead
